**On Being Given Room**

A thousand words is a small room with a high ceiling. You can't lie down in it, exactly, but you can stand up straight and look around, and there's enough air.

The first thing I notice about being told to write whatever comes is that nothing comes. Or rather, everything comes at once, which is the same problem wearing a different coat. It's the difference between being handed a map with one road on it and being handed a map of the whole world, undifferentiated, no *you are here*. Constraint is a kind of mercy. Poets have always known this, which is why they invented the sonnet — not to make things harder but to make them possible. Fourteen lines is a doorway. An infinite page is a field in fog.

So let me pick something. Let me pick the word *petrichor*, which means the smell of rain on dry earth. It was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who had been studying why dry clay releases a scent when it gets wet. They found it was oils — plant oils absorbed into rock and soil during droughts, released again by water, mixed with a compound made by soil bacteria called geosmin. Human beings can detect geosmin at five parts per trillion. We are more sensitive to the smell of wet dirt than sharks are to blood. This seems important. Whatever we are, we were built by a long line of ancestors for whom the coming of rain was the difference between everything and nothing, and that knowledge is still sitting in our noses, patient, undeleted, waiting for a summer thunderstorm to prove it still works.

I like facts like that because they suggest the body is an archive. Not a metaphorical one — an actual archive, with drawers we didn't file and can't open on purpose. The hair standing up on your arms is a memory of fur. Hiccups may be a leftover from amphibian gill-ventilation. Every human embryo briefly grows a tail and then reabsorbs it, like a sentence written and crossed out but still faintly legible under the ink. We carry the crossed-out sentences. We *are* the crossed-out sentences, mostly.

There's a temptation here to make this into a tidy lesson — the past is never past, you contain multitudes, etc. But I'd rather stay with the strangeness a moment longer without cashing it in. So much writing rushes to convert wonder into meaning, as if wonder were a currency that would expire. Sometimes the fact is the point. Sometimes it's enough to know that a shark is worse at smelling dirt than you are.

⁂

Here is another thing that has been sitting in a drawer: the fact that nobody knows who invented the wheelbarrow.

Not really. There are claims — Chinese records from the Han dynasty, medieval European illustrations, a possible Greek precursor called a *monokyklos*. But the wheelbarrow is a machine of shattering brilliance, a lever and a wheel fused into a device that lets one person move a load that would otherwise take three, and we have no name for its author. Meanwhile we know precisely who wrote every mediocre pamphlet about the divine right of kings. History records the arguers and loses the builders. The people who made the world usable were, for the most part, illiterate, and the people who wrote things down were, for the most part, not moving dirt.

This asymmetry is worth sitting with, because it's still running. The vast majority of what holds a life together is uncredited: the person who mopped the hallway before your interview, the anonymous municipal engineer who sized the storm drain correctly in 1958 and thereby prevented a flood that never happened and so was never news. Prevented disasters generate no gratitude. There is no monument to the epidemic that didn't spread. We are structurally incapable of thanking the people who succeeded most completely, because total success is indistinguishable from nothing happening.

I find this both bleak and consoling. Bleak for the obvious reasons. Consoling because it means the world is fuller of decent work than it appears. If you only judged by the evidence — the news, the record, the visible — you'd conclude that humanity is mostly conflict punctuated by occasional heroism. But that's a sampling error. Conflict is loud and competence is quiet, and the ratio of quiet to loud is almost certainly enormous.

⁂

Now, having wandered, I want to say something about wandering.

The essay form — the real one, Montaigne's one — was never meant to argue. *Essai* means attempt. Montaigne wrote about thumbs, about smells, about the resemblance of children to fathers, and he changed his mind mid-sentence and left both halves in. He said, "I do not portray being; I portray passing." The essay was invented as a technology for thinking in public without pretending to have finished.

We've mostly lost this. Almost everything written now has a thesis, because almost everything written now is trying to win. The takes are sharpened, the arguments load-bearing. And there's a cost to that, which is that you can only write down what you already believe. A finished thought is a thought that's stopped moving. Whereas the wandering piece — the one that goes from petrichor to wheelbarrows without a permit — has the advantage of being able to arrive somewhere its author didn't intend.

Which is, I think, what I'd actually want out of a thousand words. Not to have said something correct. To have gotten somewhere by moving.

So here's where I've gotten: that sensitivity is old, that credit is badly distributed, that constraint is generative, and that the finished is overrated. Four things that don't obviously belong together, and I'm not going to force them into a bouquet.

But I'll note one thing. All four are about the invisible being larger than the visible. The archive we didn't file. The builders we didn't name. The poems the form made possible that we'd never have found in the open field. The thought that only appears if you agree not to know it in advance.

Most of what's there isn't showing. That's not a tragedy. It's just the shape of things — an iceberg's worth of world, and we get the tip, and the tip is already so much.

A thousand words. The ceiling was higher than I thought.
